5.1.i: The derivative is a speedometer for a function: at each point it says how fast the output is changing compared with the input.
5.1.h: The gradient of the tangent is the limit of gradients of chords as the two points get closer. The units are always units of y per unit of x, which helps when interpreting answers.
5.1.q: V(t) is litres in a tank after t minutes, and V′(3) = −4. Interpret this.
s: Read the sign: negative means decreasing.
A derivative's sign says whether the quantity is rising or falling.
Read the units: litres per minute.
The units are y-units per x-unit.
At t = 3, the volume is decreasing at 4 litres per minute.
An interpretation needs rate, direction, units and the moment.
5.1.a: At 3 minutes the tank is losing 4 litres per minute

Derivative notation: y or f(x) the function, x the variable.
Either notation is acceptable unless a question uses one.

5.2.i: Where the gradient is positive the graph climbs, where it is negative the graph falls.
5.2.h: Sign changes in f′ can only happen where f′ = 0 or where f′ is undefined, so those points split the domain into intervals you can test one by one.
s: Solve 3x² − 12 = 0: x = ±2.
The gradient can only change sign at these values.
Test x = 0: f′(0) = −12, negative between −2 and 2.
One test value tells you the sign on the whole interval.
Outside these, f′ > 0: x < −2 or x > 2.
The derivative is an upward parabola, positive outside its roots.

5.3.i: To differentiate a power of x: bring the power down to multiply, then reduce the power by one.
5.3.h: The rule comes from expanding (x + h)ⁿ: as h → 0, only the term nxⁿ⁻¹ survives. Differentiation acts on each term separately. A constant has zero gradient, so it vanishes.
s: Rewrite −5/x² as −5x⁻².
The power rule needs terms written as powers of x.
Multiply by the power and reduce by one: −5 × −2 = +10.
The 7 becomes 0.
A constant doesn't change, so its rate of change is 0.

Power rule: a constant coefficient, n the integer power.
For terms axⁿ. Rewrite roots and fractions as powers first.

5.4.i: A tangent just touches the curve and has the curve's gradient at that point. A normal goes through the same point at right angles.
5.4.h: Both lines use one point and one gradient. The derivative gives the tangent's gradient at x = a, and the normal's gradient comes from the perpendicular rule.
5.4.q: Find the tangent and the normal to y = x² at x = 3.
s: Point: (3, 9).
A line needs a point; substitute into the original function, not the derivative.
dy/dx = 2x = 6 at x = 3.
The derivative gives the tangent's gradient at that point.
Tangent: y − 9 = 6(x − 3), so y = 6x − 9.
Point-gradient form uses what you have found.
Normal gradient −1/6: y − 9 = −(1/6)(x − 3).
Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1.

Tangent: a the x-value at the point, f(a) the y-value, f′(a) the gradient.
For a tangent at x = a.
Normal gradient: f′(a) the gradient of the tangent.
For a normal at x = a. Not defined when f′(a) = 0 (the normal is vertical).

5.5.i: Integration adds up lots of tiny pieces, which makes it the tool for area. It also reverses differentiation.
5.5.h: The constant C appears because differentiation destroys constants, so going backwards can't recover one without extra information. A definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative, so find regions separately or use |f(x)|.
5.5.q: Find the area between y = 3x² and the x-axis from x = 1 to x = 2.
s: Integrate: ∫3x² dx = x³.
Add one to the power and divide by the new power.
Evaluate: [x³] from 1 to 2 = 8 − 1 = 7.
Upper limit minus lower limit gives the accumulated area.
y > 0 on this interval, so the area is 7.
The curve stays above the axis, so the integral equals the area directly.

Power rule: a coefficient, n the power, C constant of integration.
For any n except −1. Include + C on indefinite integrals.
Area: a, b the x-limits, y the curve.

5.6.i: At the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley the curve is momentarily flat, so its gradient is zero.
5.6.h: f′(x) = 0 only finds candidates. Test the sign of f′ either side to confirm: + to − is a maximum, − to + is a minimum, no sign change is neither.
5.6.q: Find and classify the stationary point of f(x) = x² − 8x + 3.
s: Stationary points are where the gradient is zero.
The point needs a y-coordinate from the original function.
f′(3) = −2 and f′(5) = 2, so − to +: minimum.
The gradient's change in sign shows the kind of point.

5.7.i: Optimisation means finding the best value. Write what you want to maximise using one variable, then use the derivative to find its peak.
5.7.h: The constraint eliminates a variable, because the derivative method here needs a function of one variable. Check endpoints of the realistic domain too, and that the value is a max or min as required.
5.7.q: A rectangle has perimeter 40 cm. Find the maximum area.
s: The constraint lets you remove one variable.
Now the quantity to maximise depends only on x.
A maximum is at a stationary point.
A″ = −2 < 0, confirming a maximum. A = 10 × 10 = 100.
A stationary point isn't automatically a maximum, so confirm it.

5.8.i: When you can't integrate, or only have data, slice the area into strips and treat each as a trapezium.
5.8.h: Each strip has area h(y_left + y_right)/2; adding them counts interior heights twice and end heights once. A curve bending upwards puts the chords above it, giving an overestimate; downwards gives an underestimate.
5.8.q: Estimate the area with y-values 2, 3, 7 at x = 0, 1, 2.
s: The strip width is the range divided by the number of strips, not the number of points.
End heights count once, middle heights twice.
Area ≈ 7.5.
Evaluate the bracket first.

Trapezoidal rule: h strip width, n number of strips, y₀…yₙ heights.
To approximate an area from data or a difficult function.

5.9.i: These rules handle functions built from simpler ones. Chain is for one function inside another; product and quotient are for functions multiplied or divided.
5.9.h: The chain rule says rates multiply: if y changes with u and u changes with x, the changes combine. That is exactly how related-rates problems link quantities. Calculus trig results hold only in radians.
5.9.q: Differentiate y = (2x + 1)⁵ and y = x² sin x.
s: Let u = 2x + 1: dy/dx = 5u⁴ × 2.
Chain rule: differentiate the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
Replace u at the end.
For x² sin x: u = x², v = sin x.
These are two functions multiplied, so use the product rule.
dy/dx = x² cos x + 2x sin x.
Each function takes a turn being differentiated.

Standard derivatives: x in radians for the trig functions; x > 0 for ln x.
As building blocks with the rules below.
Chain rule: y a function of u, u a function of x.
For a function inside another function, and for related rates.
Product rule: When two functions of x are multiplied.
Quotient rule: u the top, v the bottom, functions of x.
When one function is divided by another. Needs v ≠ 0.

5.10.i: The second derivative says how the gradient itself is changing. It shows which way a curve bends: up like a cup or down like a cap.
5.10.h: At a stationary point, f″ > 0 means a minimum and f″ < 0 a maximum; f″ = 0 is inconclusive. A point of inflexion needs concavity to actually change, so f″ = 0 alone isn't enough.
5.10.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x, classify the stationary points.
s: Stationary points come from f′ = 0.
The second derivative tests which way the curve bends.
f″(1) = 6 > 0: minimum. f″(−1) = −6 < 0: maximum.
Concave up at the bottom of a valley; concave down at the top of a hill.
5.10.a: Minimum at x = 1; maximum at x = −1

5.11.i: Integration undoes differentiation. If the integrand looks like the result of a chain rule, there's an inside function whose derivative is also present.
5.11.h: Substitution reverses the chain rule: with u = g(x), the factor g′(x) dx becomes du. That is why the derivative must be present, up to a constant multiple.
s: Let u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx.
The inside function's derivative, 2x, is already there.
∫u³ du = u⁴/4 + C.
The substitution leaves a standard power.
Return to x, since the question was in x.

Standard integrals: x in radians for trig; C constant of integration.
As building blocks. ∫1/x is the exception to the power rule.

5.12.i: Area between curves is top minus bottom added across. A volume of revolution stacks thin circular discs along the axis.
5.12.h: Each disc has volume πy²dx, and integrating adds them. Revolving about the y-axis needs x as a function of y, with limits in y. Between two curves, subtract outer and inner volumes, never square a difference.
5.12.q: Find the volume when y = x from x = 0 to x = 3 is rotated about the x-axis.
s: V = ∫₀³ πx² dx.
Each disc has radius y = x.
V = π[x³/3] from 0 to 3.
π is a constant so it comes out.
This is a cone with r = 3 and h = 3, whose formula also gives 9π, a useful check.

Area (y-axis): a, b y-limits, x as a function of y.
For regions bounded by a curve and the y-axis.
Volume about x-axis: y as a function of x, a and b x-limits.
When rotating about the x-axis through 2π.
Volume about y-axis: x as a function of y, a and b y-limits.
When rotating about the y-axis through 2π.

5.13.i: Position, velocity and acceleration are linked by calculus. Differentiating goes from position towards acceleration, and integrating goes back.
5.13.h: Displacement is the net change, so backward motion cancels forward motion; distance adds it all up. So distance needs ∫|v| dt. Speed increases when v and a have the same sign.
5.13.q: v(t) = t − 2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. Find the displacement and the distance travelled.
s: Displacement = ∫₀⁴ (t − 2) dt = 0.
The signed integral lets motion in opposite directions cancel.
Distance = ∫₀⁴ |t − 2| dt.
Distance can't cancel, so the modulus makes all motion count.
Two triangles, each area 2, so distance = 4.
v changes sign at t = 2, and the area on each side is ½ × 2 × 2.

Kinematics: s displacement, v velocity, a acceleration, t time.
To move between s, v and a.
Distance travelled: v(t) velocity, t₁ and t₂ the times.
For total distance, always with the modulus.

5.14.i: A differential equation gives a rule for how something changes. Solving it finds the quantity itself.
5.14.h: Separating gathers each variable on its own side so that each can be integrated. Only one constant is needed. If dy/dt = ky, the rate is proportional to the amount, which leads to exponential behaviour.
5.14.q: Solve dy/dx = 2xy, with y = 3 at x = 0, for y > 0.
s: ∫(1/y) dy = ∫2x dx.
Each variable must be on its own side before integrating.
ln y = x² + C.
Integrate both sides; one constant is enough.
At x = 0, y = 3: C = ln 3.
The initial condition fixes the constant.
y = 3e^(x²).
Undo the logarithm using laws of exponents.

Separation of variables: g a function of x, h a function of y.
When dy/dx can be factorised into a part in x and a part in y.

5.15.i: A slope field is a map of short arrows showing which way a solution heads at each point. A solution curve follows the arrows like a leaf on a stream.
5.15.h: Each point has one gradient given by the differential equation. Isoclines, where the gradient is constant, help sketch quickly: dy/dx = 0 points show where solutions go flat.
5.15.q: For dy/dx = x − y, what is the gradient at (1, 3), and where are the segments horizontal?
s: At (1, 3): gradient = 1 − 3 = −2.
Substitute the point into the differential equation.
Horizontal means x − y = 0, so y = x.
A horizontal segment has gradient 0, which gives a line of such points.

5.16.i: If you can't solve a differential equation, walk along it: take the gradient where you are, take a small step in that direction, and repeat.
5.16.h: Each step follows a tangent, so errors build up where the curve bends. A smaller h means more steps and better accuracy. Coupled systems update all variables at once using the old values.
5.16.q: dy/dx = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1. Find y at x = 0.2.
s: Step along the gradient at the current point.
x moves by the step length each time.
Each new gradient uses the latest point.

Euler's method: h step length, f(x, y) the expression for dy/dx.
To approximate solutions numerically. A sequence or table on the GDC reduces errors.

5.17.i: A phase portrait shows how two linked quantities move together over time. The eigenvalues decide whether solutions head in, fly out or spiral.
5.17.h: Each eigenvector direction grows or shrinks by e^(λt). Negative real parts die away and positive ones grow. Imaginary parts cause rotation, because e^(iθ) is circular motion.
5.17.q: A system has eigenvalues 2 and −3. Describe the equilibrium at the origin.
s: The eigenvalues are real with opposite signs.
This sign pattern is what classifies the equilibrium.
e^(−3t) decays and e^(2t) grows.
Solutions approach along one eigenvector and leave along the other.
The origin is a saddle point, which is unstable.
Almost every solution is eventually pushed away.

Solution: λ₁, λ₂ eigenvalues, p₁, p₂ eigenvectors, A and B constants.
For coupled linear systems with distinct real eigenvalues.

5.18.i: A second-order equation involves acceleration. Introducing velocity as a separate variable turns one hard equation into two easy ones.
5.18.h: The trick works because Euler's method only takes first derivatives. With y = dx/dt, you step x and y forward together, using the values from the same earlier step.
5.18.q: d²x/dt² = −x, x(0) = 1, dx/dt = 0 at t = 0, h = 0.1. Find x and y after two steps.
s: Let y = dx/dt, so dy/dt = −x.
This gives two first-order equations.
Both updates use the old values.
Using the new x for y too early would be a different method.

Reduction: y = dx/dt the new variable, f the expression for the second derivative.
To apply Euler's method to second-order equations.
